pending_items.title: Israel's Eisenkot agrees to coalition deal with left-wing Democrats
pending_items.content:
The centrist party of former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot , who is trying to form the next Israeli government , and an allied left-wing party on Thursday announced they had agreed on a coalition deal.

The left-leaning Democrats are the second party to agree to a coalition deal with Eisenkot's Yashar after the right-wing Israel Beiteinu party, headed by Avigdor Lieberman , did so on Tuesday, marking a further step towards forming a government.

Eisenkot has until December 6 – a deadline which can be extended by 14 days – to form a government to replace caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after the October election failed to deliver a clear majority for either bloc.

"Gadi Eisenkot, chair of Yashar with Eisenkot, and Yair Golan, chair of the Democrats, have agreed to sign a coalition agreement between the two parties," a joint statement said on Thursday.

The Democrats said they would receive four ministerial portfolios as part of the coalition deal, including an expanded national security ministry which under Netanyahu's government is headed by the far-right Itamar Ben-Gvir .

Watch more Writer Etgar Keret: 'The Israel my parents dreamed of' is still possible, but not under Netanyahu

The party will also receive the Ministry of Labour, Ministry of Communications, and Ministry of Culture and Sport, which will include a new directorate for democracy, the party said in a statement.

"We promised the people that we ​would replace Netanyahu and defend democracy. And that is what we will do," Golan said in ‌a post on X .

"I call on all parties to come together as soon as possible to finalise agreements and sign them, form a government, and lead Israel in a new direction. This is the mission of our lives."

Eisenkot, Lieberman and Golan have a combined total of 36 lawmakers – far short of the 61 needed for a parliamentary majority.

The bloc also includes the Beyachad party of former prime minister Naftali Bennett , which has 12 seats but is yet to sign a formal coalition agreement with Yashar.

Eisenkot's wide-ranging anti-Netanyahu camp has faced divisions on whether to forge alliances with the ultra-Orthodox parties, or the Arab-majority lists, or whether to form a national unity government with Netanyahu's right-wing Likud .

The Democrats have been pushing Eisenkot for an alliance with two Arab-majority lists that achieved an unprecedented seat haul in the vote, in a bid to unseat Netanyahu.

The party disapproved of the four rounds of talks between Yashar and Likud in recent days exploring the possibility of a unity government. No breakthroughs on that front have ostensibly been reached.

Lieberman, on the other hand, has refused to serve in a government that relies on Arab-majority parties and has instead advocated an alliance with the two ultra-Orthodox parties, despite his years of criticism of the community and the fact that the issue of ultra-Orthodox military conscription remains a thorny one.

On Thursday, Lieberman warned that Netanyahu was trying to derail the government's formation.

"He will drag out negotiations over a 'unity' government until the last moment, look for a pretext to blow them up, and even if such a government is formed, he will try to engineer a crisis within a few months to drag Israel back to elections," added Lieberman, a hawkish former aide to Netanyahu who has become a strident critic.

Bennett, meanwhile, has been pushing for a unity government between Eisenkot's bloc and Likud that would exclude the ultra-Orthodox and Arab parties.

"Even at this time, I believe that by far the best alternative for the State of Israel and the serving public is a Zionist unity government led by Eisenkot first," he wrote on X, referring to a possible rotation agreement for the premiership.

pending_items.title: Exclusive-US pushed Venezuela, Iraq to consider leaving OPEC, sources say
pending_items.content:
By Ahmad Ghaddar, Ahmed Rasheed and Marianna Parraga

LONDON/BAGHDAD/HOUSTON, Nov 27 (Reuters) - The Trump administration encouraged Venezuela and Iraq to consider leaving OPEC earlier this year and prevented Venezuela from paying its annual membership dues to the group, according to ten people familiar with the matter.

The previously unreported moves targeted two of OPEC's five founding members, marking an unusually direct challenge to an organization President Donald Trump has long accused of keeping oil prices artificially high.

US officials were pushing for greater oil production and investment in both countries at the time, and some worried OPEC production limits could eventually constrain those ambitions, according to people familiar with the discussions.

The US pressure on Venezuela went far enough that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman intervened this summer, persuading the Trump administration not to press the issue further, two people familiar with the matter said.

In Iraq, Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi raised the possibility of leaving OPEC at a government meeting this summer after discussions with US officials who encouraged the idea, two people familiar with the matter said.

Iraq's oil ministry pushed back, persuading al-Zaidi to keep Iraq in the group and consider seeking a higher production quota instead, the people said.

The United States has powerful leverage over both countries. The US controls Venezuela's access to state funds following the January ouster of Nicolas Maduro, while Iraq's oil revenues continue to pass through an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, a relic of the 2003 Iraq War.

The US State Department did not answer questions about whether it had prevented Venezuela from paying its OPEC membership fee. But it confirmed Washington has the power to decide on Venezuela’s use of state funds, now held in a US-controlled account set up after Maduro's removal.

"The Department receives disbursement requests from the interim Venezuelan government and reviews the requests, including against a list of approved and prohibited uses of the foreign Government Deposit Funds," a State Department official told Reuters.

The official said that it was possible that lower-level US officials had raised the question of leaving OPEC with Venezuela's government earlier this year, but that "it has not been among the issues raised by high-level officials."

The State Department's conversations with Iraq, meanwhile, "have focused on improving energy infrastructure to increase production and transportation of energy, not OPEC," the official said.

Representatives for OPEC and for the governments of Venezuela, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia did not respond to requests for comment.

The US maneuvers add strain to an organization that has already lost four members since 2019, and whose share of the global oil market recently hit a low on the back of disruptions caused by the US and Israeli war on Iran, another OPEC founding member.

"The risk of OPEC fracture is rising," said Dan Alamariu, chief geopolitical strategist at Alpine Macro.

The United Arab Emirates announced its exit from OPEC earlier this year after becoming frustrated with the group’s production caps, while Angola, Ecuador and Qatar quit the group in 2024, 2020 and 2019, respectively. There are no indications the US was involved in those decisions.

OPEC was founded in Baghdad in September 1960 by oil producer countries seeking to assert more control over a global market that had become dominated by a small handful of Western oil companies.

Founded by Iraq, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Venezuela, OPEC is now made up of 11 members. It has also developed an alliance with several other producer countries including Russia called OPEC+, which regularly meets to decide on coordinated production levels.

Trump has repeatedly attacked OPEC throughout his decades-long business and political career, calling it a cartel and a monopoly profiting from the rest of the world. Over the past decade, though, the US has become the world's largest oil producer, turning it from an OPEC customer into its main rival for oil market share.

After the US seized Maduro in January, the US State Department opened discussions with Venezuelan officials in Washington on whether the country should leave OPEC, five people familiar with the matter told Reuters.

They did not identify the individuals who took part in those discussions.

Trump wanted US oil majors to revive Venezuela's oil output - something he said would shore up energy security in the Western Hemisphere - and worried that OPEC policy decisions could hinder that plan, the sources said.

Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman intervened, however, persuading the Trump administration not to push further, two of the sources said. Saudi Arabia is OPEC’s top producer and its de facto leader.

In August, Trump said it was up to Venezuela whether to leave OPEC.

US officials this summer also held talks with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi, encouraging Iraq's departure from OPEC as US oil majors Exxon Mobil and Chevron planned major new investments there, two people familiar with the matter said.

Al-Zaidi later raised the issue at a government meeting. His oil ministry persuaded him to stay and instead potentially seek a higher OPEC quota, they said.

The issue could come up again since some elements of Iraq’s ruling coalition are favorable to leaving OPEC and OPEC+, which they view as dominated by Saudi Arabia and Russia, the people said.

There is no indication Washington has sought to block Baghdad’s OPEC dues.

After the US invasion of Iraq in 2003, the United States began routing Iraq's oil revenues through an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. That structure remains in place more than two decades later.

This year, the US threatened to starve Iraq of its oil money if it didn’t cut Iran’s influence in its government.

OPEC membership fee payments are typically due in the first quarter of each year, and pay for staff salaries, research, and travel at the OPEC Secretariat in Vienna.

Unlike the United Nations, where dues are scaled to the size of a country's economy, OPEC splits the fees equally among members at around 2.8 million euros ($3.08 million) each.

The price tag is tiny compared to OPEC oil revenues, but paying it carries symbolic importance as a marker of continued membership in an organization Caracas helped create.

Washington argued money from Venezuela could be spent on more important matters, one of the people familiar with the country's relationship with OPEC said.

OPEC has the discretion to disregard unpaid membership fees, and is not planning to expel Venezuela over the issue, two OPEC sources told Reuters.

Washington's control of Venezuela's oil revenues and finances has led some in the South American country to refer to their country as a US protectorate, instead of a sovereign nation.

The US Government Accountability Office opened a formal investigation in July into the administration’s management and disbursement of Venezuelan oil revenues, following congressional requests for transparency.

The Trump administration has said Venezuela's oil revenues are being used to meet the needs of the Venezuelan people, including to pay government salaries and fund essential services.

Reuters could not establish when exactly the US rejected the OPEC dues payment request.

Venezuela is currently exempt from OPEC+ oil output quotas as its production has collapsed from historical highs due to years of sanctions and mismanagement.

The country pumped about 1.2 million barrels per day in September, according to OPEC figures. Its state oil company PDVSA has said it plans to reach 1.5 million bpd by the end of next year.

OPEC last regulated Caracas' output with quotas in 2017-2018 when the country’s target was around 2 million bpd. The country's return to the quota system is unlikely until it hits that level again, a source familiar with Venezuela's OPEC position said.

(Additional reporting by Jonathan Saul and Timothy Gardner; Writing by Alex Lawler and Dmitry Zhdannikov; Editing by Veronica Brown and Richard Valdmanis)

pending_items.title: ‘You can’t stop it’: Indians embrace Pakistani dramas, defying bans
pending_items.content:
When New Delhi-based cultural impresario and curator Abu Sufiyan Khan organised a recent screening of the Pakistani romantic drama Dar-e-Nijaat in the Indian capital, he was stunned. It was meant to be a private event for 45 people, at most. Khan got more than 700 requests for attendance.

Like all other Pakistani shows and songs, Dar-e-Nijaat is officially banned in India. Yet every weekend, Indian viewers gather on Instagram to exchange clips, debate episodes and celebrate its leading character, Abu Bakr.

Offline, watch parties and group screenings are organised in different parts of the country. As the craze for the show – which involves a young woman Zaryab, her childhood love Zamil, and Abu Bakr, who later steps into Zaryab’s life to fill a void – has gripped Indian cities, the police have been left playing cat-and-mouse.

At least two screenings in the southern city of Bengaluru, scheduled for this coming weekend, have now been cancelled after authorities saw posters advertising the events. But those attempts at a crackdown haven’t dimmed the appeal of the show.

One phrase, repeated across fan pages and comment sections, has become a shorthand for its craze: “Sabr ka phal nahi, Abu Bakr chahiye,” (We don’t want the reward of patience; we want Abu Bakr.)

It is a playful twist on a familiar Urdu proverb, and an indication of the affection Indian viewers have developed for a fictional Pakistani man. “We have all been looking forward to an Abu Bakr. I have been going gaga over him because of how empathetic he is, and that is what is missing in most of the men these days,” says Rakhshanda Mujib, a fan from Bengaluru.

Yet the excitement over Dar-e-Nijaat is only the latest expression of a much wider appetite. India’s efforts to keep Pakistani entertainment off its screens have done little to extinguish the appetite for it.

“Indians cannot approach Pakistani artists on Instagram, access Pakistani music on Spotify or view Pakistani dramas without VPNs or proxies on YouTube,” Sufiyan Khan said.

But for many, the forbidden fruit of Pakistani culture remains alluring enough to risk breaching the official ban.

Despite multiple wars and near-perpetual tensions, India and Pakistan had for decades allowed cultural exchanges – even though they each periodically imposed restrictions.

But informal bans on Pakistani artistes working or performing in India gained ground over the past decade as Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government in New Delhi increasingly dialled down all contact with Pakistan to a bare minimum.

A new tipping point arrived in April 2025, when gunmen killed 26 tourists in Pahalgam, in Indian-administered Kashmir. India blamed Pakistan for the attack, while Islamabad denied any role. The neighbours fought an intense four-day war before agreeing to a ceasefire.

Since then, India has banned all Pakistani songs, movies and dramas from streaming platforms, including YouTube. It has cited national security for its decision. This week, it demanded that Netflix take down – from viewing in India – Pakistan’s first show on that platform.

Yet while China imposed a similar ban on Korean pop culture in 2016, and it held for the better part of a decade, India’s efforts appear to be failing.

The reason lies in where the chokepoint sits. China controls the platforms its citizens use. India does not control YouTube. Section 69A of India’s Information Technology Act lets the government direct platforms to block content, and the orders are generally confidential. In practice, YouTube geo-blocked Pakistani channels for users in India.

But a geo-block governs a platform, not a viewer. A VPN changes where a viewer appears to be, and anyone who downloads a drama that way can re-upload it from an account inside India.

On May 8, 2025 – the day streaming platforms were told to drop Pakistani content – searches for VPNs in India rose 72 percent, according to the monitoring firm Top10VPN, which links the rise to both governments blocking each other’s online content.

Those VPNs downloaded in India translate into good business for Pakistani channels like ARY Digital, the network behind Dar-e-Nijaat.

“Indian viewers account for 30 to 35 percent of total views for Pakistani channels”, says Jerjees Seja, head of ARY Entertainment. “In this day and age, you can make access to content difficult, but you can’t stop it.”

Seja’s assertion is hard to dispute. The 2022 drama Tere Bin and the 2024 soap Kabhi Main Kabhi Tum were both also wildly popular in India. Pakistani director Mehreen Jabbar says viewers in India message her about her series such as Dr Bahu, Jackson Heights and Daam.

So, what makes these shows click for Indian audiences?

Culturally, the similarities between India and Pakistan mean that a lot that’s seen in Pakistani shows is instantly relatable for many across the border. Seja adds that Pakistan’s entertainment industry has also grown in its quality of production. “Our content has become very strong over the years,” he said. “It is realistic, on-the-ground, thought-provoking, and relatable.”

But there’s another reason, too, suggests Sufiyan Khan, that dramas like Dar-e-Nijaat find a willing audience in India. Far too often, Indian shows and movies stereotype Muslim characters. By contrast, Dar-e-Nijaat’s appeal, he said, lies in part in its “exceptional portrayal of Islam as not being threatening or Bollywood-style performative with kohl eyes and prayer caps but a refreshing, non-judgmental and inclusive Islam where all the rituals are being practised with humility”.

Culture is inconvenient in wartime politics because it makes an enemy familiar. But technology has made it harder for governments to firewall entire societies.

“Over the last few years, a whole wave of Indian people are consuming Pakistani TV shows, music and influencer content. There has been a democratisation of culture and access, which has led to the breaking of stereotypes,” said Aishwarya Verma, a policy analyst in Delhi. “Back in the day, we didn’t know too much about our brothers and sisters across the border, and vice versa.”

Pakistani actress and singer Haniya Aamer, for instance, is popular for her music in India. A recent song by her, Pablo, features Indian actress Rakhi Sawant. “We’re all listening to her music,” said Verma. “Who would have thought?”

Ajay Bisaria, former Indian high commissioner to Pakistan, said bans of the kind India has imposed rarely work. “Technology changes. It makes both borders and bans less relevant. Governments impose bans because culture is visible and easy to restrict. Pakistan has done the same: Indian films were banned there for decades.”

Yet, as with Pakistani shows in India, Bollywood thrived on pirated cassettes in Pakistan.

“Culture”, Bisaria said, “has played a massive binding force in the bilateral relationship between India and Pakistan, whether the two nations have wanted it or not.” And Dar-e-Nijaat shows it continues to do so.

pending_items.title: Can the Mecca pact turn its collective defence promise into real support?
pending_items.content:
Islamabad, Pakistan – Senior officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye are meeting in Islamabad on Friday to discuss their Mecca defence pact , as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and sporadic Iranian strikes on other Gulf countries continue.

The officials are meeting for the third time since the three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on August 7 , under which an armed attack on one member is treated as an attack on all three.

The agreement was signed amid a wider war that began with United States-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.

Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif told the AFP news agency earlier this week that the “continuous turmoil south of Saudi Arabia” – a reference to Yemen, where the Houthis are based – would be on the agenda. He confirmed that the defence and foreign ministers of all three countries would attend the Islamabad meeting.

“Any threat to Saudi Arabia is a threat to Pakistan and Turkiye according to the pact, which is absolutely clear,” Asif said.

He described the pact as still being at an early stage.

“Initially we need to have frequent meetings to steer what is being formulated, in a way that in the next couple of months we have everything in place so that we can move forward,” he said.

Pakistan has pledged to defend Saudi territory but has ruled out attacking the Houthis inside Yemen.

Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs set out that boundary on October 9. Spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said Pakistani troops stationed in Saudi Arabia under the alliance would not cross into Yemen to attack the Houthis .

“It is an alliance intended to defend the three countries against aggression,” he said at the weekly news briefing.

On April 11, as Islamabad hosted talks between US and Iranian officials aimed at ending the war, Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Defence said a Pakistani force , including fighter and support aircraft, had arrived at King Abdulaziz airbase in the country’s Eastern Province under a bilateral mutual defence agreement that Islamabad and Riyadh had signed in 2025.

Muhammad Faisal, a Sydney-based security and foreign policy analyst, said much of the Pakistani military presence in Saudi Arabia rested on that older bilateral arrangement .

“Importantly, Pakistan’s existing military presence and defence coordination with Saudi Arabia largely predate the Mecca Pact,” he told Al Jazeera, referring to the bilateral mutual defence pact inked in September 2025, at a time when Gulf countries were reevaluating their dependence on US security guarantees after Israel struck Qatar.

Faisal added that Riyadh had not publicly pressed Islamabad to take part in offensive operations inside Yemen.

But Umer Karim, an associate fellow at the King Faisal Center for Research and Islamic Studies in Riyadh, said that limit fell short of what Saudi Arabia wanted.

Therein lies a dilemma, both for Pakistan and for Saudi Arabia: The deeper Pakistan becomes involved against the Houthis, Karim said, the weaker its diplomatic role would become in US-Iran mediation and in its more recent efforts to mediate between Iran and Saudi Arabia. That’s because Iran is the principal external backer of the Houthis.

“Saudi Arabia wants Pakistan to contribute to its defence against the Houthis, and perhaps to act more against the Houthis in an offensive manner, but it also wants to retain Pakistan as a conduit of diplomatic engagement with Iran,” he told Al Jazeera.

On November 24, the Saudi Civil Defence said 11 people were injured when a tower in Riyadh’s financial centre was hit in a Houthi attack.

At least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi drone and missile attacks in Saudi Arabia since September 23, according to Saudi authorities. Twenty-three of them were killed in strikes on airports.

At an emergency meeting of the pact’s member countries in Riyadh on October 5, the committee agreed to provide forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom.

The joint statement did not name Yemen or the Houthis.

On November 21, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan told Turkish media: “Our current policy is aimed at the defence of Saudi Arabia; no decision has been made on deploying troops inside Yemen. However, the necessary support is being provided in defending Saudi Arabia.”

Omer Ozkizilcik, an Ankara-based analyst and nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, expected the alliance to remain defensive for the moment.

“As of now, as the Saudis only requested defensive support, I do not expect the Mecca Pact to get involved in offensive military operations against the Houthi militias in Yemen,” he told Al Jazeera.

Nawaf Obaid, a senior research fellow at the Department of War Studies at King’s College London, outlined the scope of Pakistan’s commitment.

“Pakistan’s military commitment to the defence of Saudi Arabia encompasses capabilities across the land and air domains, including combat aviation, ground formations, integrated air and missile defence, and geospatial intelligence support. Defensive military operations can involve direct combat,” he told Al Jazeera.

The Riyadh meeting was also attended by retired Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood, a former three-star Pakistani general, who was appointed earlier in September as the alliance’s first secretary-general for a three-year term.

The secretariat is based in Riyadh, where Mahmood met Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud on November 19 to review efforts to build the alliance’s institutional framework, according to the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said on October 23 that Islamabad and Riyadh had completed their ratification processes. T urkiye’s parliament approved the agreement on November 5 by 279 votes to 119. On Friday, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan signed off on the ratification.

Eyup Ersoy, a visiting research fellow at Pembroke College, University of Oxford, said the alliance had moved quickly.

“The speed and scale of the formation of legal and institutional foundations of the agreement so far attest to the noteworthy performance of the agreement as well,” he told Al Jazeera.

Ozkizilcik, however, pointed to its limits.

“The Mecca Pact does not include a superpower. So, its capabilities and power projections will always be limited, in that it’s an alliance of regional or middle powers,” he said.

The alliance has not publicly detailed how it would decide on a joint military response, which forces it would call on or who would command them.

On October 26 , Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir, and Turkiye’s intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, in Tehran.

That meeting is widely believed to have been facilitated by Islamabad. “This showcased Pakistan’s dual role as an active member of the Mecca alliance and a diplomatic bridge between Riyadh and Tehran,” Faisal, the Sydney-based analyst, said.

Obaid said Tehran understood Pakistan’s position.

“Pakistan is not strategically neutral when it comes to Saudi Arabia and Iran, and the Iranians understand this perfectly well. Islamabad has an immediate national security interest in preventing a renewed military confrontation between the United States and Iran, which explains its mediation efforts,” he said.

On October 31, Rezaei told Iranian state television that Prince Khalid had warned that Israel would go after Turkiye once it was done with Iran, and then Saudi Arabia. Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad have not publicly commented on his account.

Javad Heiran-Nia, director of the Persian Gulf Studies Group in Tehran, said Iran viewed the pact through that lens.

“Iran welcomes any mechanism that creates a balance against Israel and weakens the American order in the region,” he told Al Jazeera, even as Tehran “knows that one dimension of the Mecca Pact, and of possible participation in it, is to control Iran and its proxy forces”.

At a weekly briefing on November 20, Pakistani spokesperson Khan said the agreement “is defensive in nature and is not directed against any country”.

The text of the agreement, as submitted to the Turkish parliament , names no country or region as a threat.

Asif declined to tell AFP how the pact would respond to a direct Iranian attack on Saudi Arabia. He named Israel as a possible threat to the region.

“The possibility of some conflict, or aggression from the Israeli side exists, so we need to close our ranks, the countries of this region,” he said.

Karim, from the King Faisal Center for Research and Islamic Studies, said pressure on Pakistan could grow if Riyadh’s outreach to Tehran stalled.

“Once Saudi Arabia recognises diplomatic engagement with Iran is not bringing any meaningful outcomes, only then perhaps will it further pressure Pakistan to be more openly involved against the Houthis, which would indeed imperil its goodwill with Iran,” he said.

pending_items.title: Hakeem Jeffries has disarmed a progressive revolt, but can he deliver?
pending_items.content:
The overwhelming blue wave of the 2026 United States midterm elections should have simply been seen as a crowning achievement for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries that propelled him into the position of next speaker of the House of Representatives. And while that outcome appears all but guaranteed now that he has secured more than enough support from the incoming House Democratic Caucus, Jeffries’ ascent to the top House leadership position has been significantly rockier than anticipated.

The blue wave was, in part, a progressive and anti-establishment phenomenon. And while we in the media have likely exaggerated the impact of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) in this year’s election cycle, DSA-affiliated and other newly elected far-left lawmakers have already asserted themselves as a vocal minority amongst the incoming House Democratic Caucus. They’ve done so by calling on the party to move left on issues such as healthcare, campaign finance and America’s relationship with Israel. And these newly elected progressives have also targeted congressional leaders, namely Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who they see as embodying the party’s status quo.

Jeffries has reached the pinnacle of power within his party by being a shrewd political operator who has deftly managed the leverage of the Democratic minority in the closely divided House. His handling of the recent challenge to his leadership shows that he remains a step ahead of his opponents within the party. Jeffries declined the opportunity to be chosen by acclamation, an option that could have allowed him to gloss over the opposition to his speakership. Instead, Jeffries insisted on a formal secret ballot. The choice was strategic. Much like a prime minister calling for early elections, he organised the vote to happen before progressive opposition had coalesced around a single candidate (unlike in the Senate, where Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen is amassing support to challenge Schumer). The move represented a tactic Jeffries observed while under the wing of Nancy Pelosi, who called a similar vote in 2018 after her leadership was challenged by vocal incoming members of Congress. In the end, potential challengers for the role of speaker, such as Representatives Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts and Jamie Raskin of Maryland, declined to throw their hats in the ring to run against Jeffries. The vast majority of the caucus fell in line behind the New York congressman, with 251 votes in favour and only 11 against, the latter largely from incoming DSA-aligned representatives-elect.

For Jeffries, the progressive revolt against his leadership has been, in the short term, a mere speed bump on his path to becoming speaker. In the longer term, those 11 “no” votes represent a more significant progressive challenge to Jeffries’ record and agenda that will not easily disappear. However, the presumptive next speaker of the House is poised to overcome this challenge, as his skill as a political operative, the relatively weak position of his progressive opposition, and the historic nature of Jeffries’ leadership all work in his favour.

Over the course of the 2026 election cycle, Jeffries secured the support of important progressive figures, including fellow New Yorkers such as New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. During the brief post-election speculation over his leadership, the New York congressman also won over progressives including Texas Representative Greg Casar, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus. Jeffries’ predecessor as Democratic leader, Pelosi, was able to manage dissent from the progressive Squad through a combination of personal relationships and strategic committee assignments that channelled their energies toward oversight of the executive branch. Jeffries may likewise seek to manage the “Bloc”, as the new progressives are being called by some, in similar fashion.

Meanwhile, Jeffries’ primary message since the midterm elections has been one of affordability, a potent message that has resonated with voters across the political spectrum and thus can unite centrists and progressives within the Democratic Party. The speaker-designate has also signalled that he is willing to move in the direction of progressives’ concerns on substantive issues. Most notably, on November 17, the eve of the speaker nomination vote, Jeffries endorsed a plan to expand Medicare by lowering the age of eligibility for older Americans, covering children under 18, and including dental, vision and hearing coverage. This new “Medicare for more” plan, coupled with rolling back Trump-era cuts to Medicaid and restoring Affordable Care Act tax credits, has been gaining steam among both centrists and progressives. The latter have framed it as a quickly achievable first step towards Medicare for All. Both progressive elder statesman Senator Bernie Sanders and members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus have adopted this rhetoric.

Whether this “first step” framing is accurate is unknowable. The Affordable Care Act was presented in similar terms, but the progressive aim to use Obamacare as a foundation to build a universal healthcare system did not materialise over the subsequent decade. However, the willingness of major progressive forces to adopt the narrative seems to be opening space for Jeffries to navigate. This undercuts the power that the incoming progressives have to make healthcare a major dividing issue within the Democratic caucus.

Jeffries also has the power of history on his side. The congressman from Brooklyn is poised to take control of the top House spot as the chamber’s first Black speaker. He will be backed by an unprecedented slate of diverse leaders within the Democratic House Caucus, with historic firsts for Black, Hispanic and Asian legislators, among others. Even President Donald Trump acknowledged Jeffries’ personal acumen and the historic nature of becoming the first Black speaker, calling it “a big deal”, and referring to Jeffries as “a very smart guy”. Jeffries has in turn signalled a willingness to work with members of the Trump administration, though not with new White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, who Jeffries calls a “stone-cold racist”.

Black candidates and Black voters played huge roles in Democrats’ 2026 surge in ways that have not neatly mapped onto the “centrist insiders v. progressive outsiders” narrative that has defined the party’s main internal division. Though Black Democrats and progressives are by no means mutually exclusive wings of the party, the far left has sometimes had difficulties appealing to Black voters. As such, progressives face potential backlash if they are perceived as attempting to prevent or hamstring the leadership of the first Black speaker of the House. Already, some of the attacks against Jeffries have been condemned for racist language and undertones. Progressives run the risk of being tone-deaf and appearing on the wrong side of history, meaning that they will have to tread lightly if they continue to question Jeffries’ leadership.

In the short run, Jeffries has made the right moves politically and leaned into the importance of the moment, all while solidifying his coalition and moving leftward in a way that balances progressive priorities with legislative practicality. Whether he can temper progressive demands and maintain a unified caucus may depend on forces outside of his control. In terms of Democrats’ domestic agenda, incoming Senate sensation and Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed is becoming the face of the Medicare for All movement, even pushing for a long-shot deal with President Trump on the issue. Growing momentum within the Senate could push the issue beyond Jeffries’ ability to manage. Similarly, in a recent New York Times interview, Jeffries signalled a willingness to walk a tightrope between holding the Trump administration accountable and working with the White House and other Republicans. But this balancing act may prove untenable if the continued lawlessness of Trump and his cabinet leads to intensified demands for investigations and even impeachments.

And foreign affairs may be an even larger stumbling block for Jeffries, who has come under fire for his support for Israel as sentiment grows in both parties to re-evaluate the US relationship with its longtime Middle East ally. For now, Jeffries has gotten some cover by gaining the support of figures like Mamdani, a vocal and credible critic of the genocidal war in Gaza and of Israel’s treatment of Palestinians. But in that same New York Times interview, Jeffries prevaricated when asked about accepting AIPAC funding in the future or pushing for legislation that would cut weapons sales to Israel and impose sanctions on entities tied to illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Again, Jeffries appears to be offering a compromise, promoting the less forceful West Bank Settler Violence Protection and Prevention Act, which targets the sponsors of settler pogroms but not the underlying scheme of settlement itself in Palestinian territory. It’s less clear that such a stance will be enough to satisfy Jeffries’ left flank. However, the growing controversy over AIPAC led the pro-Israel lobbying group, even prior to November’s election results, to shift its strategy of supporting candidates to a model that emphasises individual donors rather than direct political action committee funding for campaigns. The electoral shellacking that AIPAC-backed candidates experienced in the midterm elections may further lead the lobbying organisation to take a less high-profile approach going forward, which could help to slightly tone down Israel’s prominence in US politics.

For the time being, the Iran war is the more pressing foreign policy concern, and this will be one of Jeffries’ first major tests. He has pledged to prioritise ending the war, a popular stance that could be another unifying position for centrists, progressives and even some Republican lawmakers. But the speaker-designate has already been criticised for indicating that he might be willing to cut a temporary budget deal with Republicans that keeps money flowing to the war rather than using the leverage of a government shutdown to insist on cutting funds for the conflict. Even Trump and Vice President JD Vance have acknowledged the Iran war as a major reason behind Republicans’ 2026 defeats. Failure by Jeffries to take bold action against the conflict now will be seen as a missed opportunity and create a new opening for progressives to question his fitness to lead in this moment.

After securing the nomination for speaker, Jeffries surprised the incoming Democratic House caucus with a visit by former President Barack Obama, to whom Jeffries has been compared before. Obama was a unique leader who combined a principled pragmatism with an unmatched ability to inspire, and he urged the new Democratic representatives to stick to their principles while learning how to “get s*** done” with colleagues who had different points of view. Jeffries leans more toward Obama’s pragmatism than his idealism, and his penchant for practicality at the expense of vision may be the presumptive speaker’s greatest strength and biggest liability. Even if he is willing to compromise with the left wing of his party, Jeffries will not be the bold visionary that progressives want leading the House. But with domestic and foreign concerns to address such as healthcare and the war with Iran, Jeffries has the chance to be the leader who gets things done. Jeffries will have the next two years to accomplish these and other goals for the party and its supporters. Whether or not he delivers results on these issues, and how voters assess the party’s performance come 2028, will make or break Jeffries’ speakership.

pending_items.title: Western sanctions on Israeli settlers serve to shield the Israeli state
pending_items.content:
On November 17, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman, Fadda Fheidat, was shot in the head and killed as she stood outside her home in al-Duyuk at-Tahta in Jericho. Fadda was murdered by Israeli settlers, who had recently forcibly evicted at least 13 Palestinian households from their homes in the neighbourhood.

What makes this takeover so significant is the location: the outskirts of Jericho, widely described as the world’s oldest continuously inhabited city and the first city to be handed over to the newly established Palestinian Authority in 1994 following the Oslo Accords.

Hours after Fadda was killed, Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich visited the new settlement outpost and praised the settlers for what he characterised as a renewal of Jewish settlement in Jericho. It is the first Israeli settlement established inside a Palestinian city in the West Bank since settlers established a presence in the heart of Hebron nearly five decades ago.

This latest settler takeover was spearheaded by the far-right settler organisation Nachala with the support of the settler Binyamin Regional Council. Nachala was founded by the fanatical settler Daniella Weiss and has long campaigned for the ethnic cleansing and settlement of all of historic Palestine. Weiss and her organisation have gained international notoriety as a result of their relentless campaign calling for the Israeli government to complete the mass expulsion of Palestinians from Gaza and settle the area with Israelis.

Albeit politically significant, the takeover of homes in Jericho is not surprising. Since the genocide in Gaza began more than three years ago, Israeli settler takeover of Palestinian homes and land has drastically escalated in the West Bank. More than 6,000 Palestinians – half of whom are children – have been forcibly expelled as a result. The Israeli military has also been conducting its own expulsions. Between January and February 2025, the Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarem refugee camps in the northern West Bank were emptied of their populations – some 33,000 residents.

One cannot separate the actions of the settlers and the military. The two work hand in glove towards their ultimate goal, which is to force as many Palestinians as possible off the land.

Both actors are part of a larger settler-colonial structure which enables this accelerating expansion. Indeed, the majority of settlements in the West Bank are connected to Israeli regime infrastructure, including Israeli-only roads and water and electricity networks, and many offer state subsidies as incentives for Jewish Israelis to live there. When one sees the settlements with one’s own eyes, it is clear that there is no separation between them and the Israeli state.

Yet the distinction between settlers and the settler-colonial structure is a useful tool for Israel’s more liberal supporters. To blame the settlers and a few more extreme ministers is to provide a scapegoat for the structure that masquerades as the only liberal democracy in the region.

We can see this scapegoating in how some Western governments have responded to settlement expansion. For example, both Nachala and Weiss have been sanctioned by the UK, Australia, Canada and the European Union – sanctions that include asset freezes and travel bans. Sanctions like this effectively allow governments to claim action, when in reality, the impact on the ground is limited.

This distinction between settlers and the Israeli regime is also evident in the language used to announce the sanctions. In her November 18 statement announcing the sanctions, Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong failed to mention the Israeli government at all: “We are taking these actions because the rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution”.

Some might argue that freezing settler assets and imposing travel bans is at least a step in the right direction. But this is a naive outlook. Limited sanctions like these are a politically calculated tactic. In the UK, growing anger among the British public over their government’s complicity in the genocide necessitated a response from the incoming prime minister, Andy Burnham.

Yet when his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced earlier this year the new approach the UK government was taking vis-à-vis Palestine and Israel, it was reported that British officials were also working to de-escalate tensions and give assurances to the Israeli government that the sanctions would be limited in scope.

Indeed, the earlier sanctions did nothing to stop what happened in al-Duyuk at-Tahta, where Palestinians were evicted from their homes by settlers, supported by soldiers and praised by government ministers. In fact, the settler movement appears to be intact and growing in support and power every day.

This is why sanctions cannot be limited to individual actors and organisations – they need to be comprehensively applied to the structure behind them. But that requires a moral backbone and political courage – something that seems to be completely lacking on the international stage.
